paragraphs.text: Dear elders and sisters, sorry that this is so late. It has been a busy day. Well, things seem to be speeding up. We spent part of the afternoon and evening at the MTC last night and really enjoyed visiting with the missionaries that were there. They're so excited to get back into the mission field. I mean, they're in the mission field, but they're not in the mission field and they know that and they're just, they're hungry. They're hungry for news about what missionaries like you are doing. So it was fun to be with them.

As you all know, the NCR went to G.C.Q. today. Unfortunately, there's been a big spike up in the last few days of new cases. So there are some rumors out there that we might go back to E.C.Q. but I'm going to stay hopeful and positive and I suggest you do the same because, hey, we don't know what's going to happen. So we might as well be positive because it feels better, right?

Listen, I want to talk to you a little bit about integrity. You know, this is something that I talk a lot about because you've come to this stage in your life where it really comes down to you being honest with you. If you're honest with yourself, you're always going to be honest with everybody else. But dishonesty and lack of integrity always starts with yourself. And that's where you want to be careful. So you want to watch yourself. Like King Benjamin says in the final few verses of his great speech to the people of his time, you know, you got to watch yourself, watch what you're thinking, what you're doing, watch what you're saying because it's really easy, very, very easy to get on that slippery slope, that slippery mountainside. And once you're on it, you just can't stop the sliding. You just end up sliding lower and lower and lower.

So I want to share a couple of stories with you. These are true stories that have been inspiring to me. The first one is about a gangster. There was a gangster in Chicago back about 100 years ago by the name of Al Capone. And he was an incredible genius when it came to crime. I mean, no one could catch him. The authorities knew that he was the gang leader of this humongous sort of criminal enterprise in Chicago. Pretty much owned Chicago. I mean, owned the politicians. He was in control of things. And the different law enforcement people tried to catch him, but they just never catch him. He had a lawyer who was brilliant and the lawyer had a name, Easy Eddie. And he was Al Capone's lawyer because he was such a good lawyer. Eddie's skills in legal tricks kept Al Capone from going to prison. And Al Capone showed his appreciation for Easy Eddie because he just showered him with money and every luxury in life that could be enjoyed, including a gated mansion with servants. So his lawyer was living in this mansion that entirely filled up a whole Chicago city block. That's how big this guy's estate was that Al Capone gave him because he was such a good lawyer at getting Al Capone out of trouble.

Eddie lived this high life. He gave very little thought to the evils that went on all around him and that, frankly, he was allowing to continue by his legal trickery. But he did have one soft spot in his heart. He had a son that he just loved completely. And he really did everything he could to help his son get what he needed in life to get ahead. But as Eddie grew older and he saw what he was becoming, he wanted his son not to be like this. He tried to teach his son right from wrong. He wanted his son to be a better man than he was. And yet with all of his wealth and influence, there were two things that Eddie just couldn't give to a son. He couldn't give his son a good example and he couldn't give his son a good name because that son would always be known as the son of Easy Eddie, the guy who got Al Capone off from all of the crimes that he had done.

It was later in life that Easy Eddie finally decided to do the right thing and to try to fix it all. And he went to the law, to law enforcement, and he told the truth about Al Capone in hopes that it would kind of make up for all of the things that he had done wrong and maybe be an example of integrity to his son. In order to do this, he knew he would have to testify against Al "Scarface" Capone and the mob, and that it would probably cost him dearly, maybe cost him his life. But he had the integrity finally to be the kind of example, the kind of father that his son deserved. And so he testified. Within a year, Easy Eddie was killed in a blaze of gunfire on a lonely Chicago street. In his eyes, he had given the greatest gift he could to his son. Police pulled from his pocket a rosary, a crucifix, a religious medallion, and a poem that he had clipped from a magazine. The poem read this way: "The clock of life is wound but once, and no man has the power to tell just when the hands will stop at late or early hour. Now is the only time you own, live, love, toil with a will, place no faith in time, for the clock may soon be still." And of course, the clock did still for Easy Eddie, but at least before it came to its end, he had done the right thing. He had set an example for his son.

The second story comes from World War Two. There were many, many heroes in World War Two and many, many heroes right here in the Philippines in World War Two. Some great stories from Filipino fighters that fought the Japanese at tremendous sacrifice. But one such hero that I want to tell you about is Lieutenant Butch O'Hare, a fighter pilot. One day his entire squadron was sent on a mission. After being airborne, he looked down at his fuel gauge and to his surprise, he realized that the crew on the aircraft carrier had forgotten to top off his fuel tank. As a result, he would not have enough fuel to complete his mission and get back to the ship. He was told by his commander on the radio to return to the ship immediately. He did so reluctantly and dropped out of the formation and started to head back to the ship.

As he was returning, he saw something that turned his blood cold. A Japanese squadron was speeding towards the American fleet. And with all the airplanes off the ships, the American fleet was defenseless. He had no time to bring his squadron back to help and he had no way of warning the fleet of his approaching danger, of that approaching danger. There was only one thing he could do and that was to try to divert all those Japanese fighter planes from the fleet. Not taking into account his own personal safety, he dove into the formation of Japanese planes with his wing-mounted guns blazing as he surprised one enemy plane after another. When his ammunition ran out, he dove at enemy planes with the hopes of clipping a wing and sending them downward. And finally, the surprised and frustrated Japanese squadron took off in another direction.

Well, Butch O'Hare and his battered fighter limped back to the aircraft carrier. Once he landed, he told of his adventure and the film from his gun camera mounted on the plane told the whole story and the extent of Butch's heroism. He had destroyed five enemy aircraft and because of his actions, he became the United States Navy's first ace of World War II and the first naval aviator to win the Congressional Medal of Honor, the highest award granted to anybody in military service in the United States. A year later, at age 29, Butch was killed in another aerial combat. His hometown would not allow his memory to fade. And today, the big airport in Chicago is called the O'Hare Airport. I've flown in and out of Chicago O'Hare Airport many times, having never ever known that story. It's named after Butch because of his bravery and his integrity.

So what do these two stories have in common? Well, pretty simply, Butch O'Hare was Easy Eddie's son. You see what an example can do? You see what a name can do? Elders and sisters, I hope that you will consider what you do because each day as we do the things that we do, we're painting the tapestry of our lives. And who knows but what we will someday have our own children who will look to our example in their moments of greatest danger and greatest temptation. And if your example has been one of integrity, one of honesty, one of courage, they will find strength from seeing your example. I hope these will be useful to you as you ponder these two true stories. Enjoy a good night's rest. Work hard tomorrow. Make it a great day. Love y'all.
